227	## Criteria
228	
229	Apply all six criteria in the order listed. Criteria 1-5 follow the order of the
230	six-section output format — the same chain-of-artifacts sequence the analysis itself
231	follows — so that a scoring pass moves through the analysis in the order it was produced;
232	Criterion 6 is a whole-document cross-section check applied last.
233	
234	### Criterion 1: Identify Essence
235	
236	Scores the **Essence Statement** — the single sentence naming the core problem followed by
237	a short list of success criteria — in the Problem Essence section (output section 1).
238	
239	- **Rigorous** — the Essence Statement is a single sentence that names the core question or
240	  decision (not a symptom, not the triggering event, not a restatement of the user's prompt);
241	  each success criterion contains a pass/fail structural test — a verb + subject + outcome
242	  triplet where the outcome is a property of the Conclusion section — so that a reviewer
243	  applies each criterion by scanning the Conclusion section without analyst interpretation;
244	  the statement is specific enough that it appears nowhere in an analysis of a different but
245	  related problem without modification (it names a property unique to this problem, not a
246	  generic template phrase).
247	  If this section uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`), the
248	  stated reason is specific to this analysis's problem — it names a property of the problem
249	  that makes an Essence Statement unnecessary or redundant, and that reason appears in no
250	  other analysis without alteration.
251	
252	- **Sound** — the Essence Statement exists and names a question, but the success criteria are
253	  vague or stated in terms that cannot be verified against the conclusion without further
254	  clarification (e.g., "the solution should be good," "the approach should be appropriate").
255	
256	- **Hand-wavy** — the Essence Statement exists but names a symptom, a triggering event, or a
257	  restatement of the user's prompt rather than the underlying question; OR the success criteria
258	  are absent while the Essence Statement itself is present; OR the section uses the honest-depth
259	  escape valve with a reason that is generic and would apply equally to any analysis (e.g.,
260	  "no essence was needed").
261	
262	- **Absent** — no Essence Statement is present (the Problem Essence section is empty, contains
263	  only a restatement of the original prompt with no analytical distillation, or the section
264	  heading appears with nothing below it).
265	  This verdict routes back to Phase 1 to re-frame the Essence Statement — or, when the cause is an input that was never supplied, to re-opening input under the Input Contract — rather than an in-place rewrite of output section 1; the route is bounded by the same rule described under `SKILL.md`'s "Before presenting conclusions" section.
266	
267	### Criterion 2: Challenge Assumptions
268	
269	Scores the **Classified Assumptions Table** — a table with columns Assumption, Type, Treatment,
270	Verdict, Verification — in the Assumptions Table section (output section 2). Folds in:
271	four-type classification quality and unverified-flag discipline (D-07).
272	
273	- **Rigorous** — every row in the Assumptions Table has a Type value drawn from exactly the
274	  four-type scheme (physical law / current constraint / convention / untested belief); the
275	  Treatment cell uses the vocabulary of the prescribed treatment for that type; the Verdict
276	  cell records Accept, Challenge, or Discard as a leading token followed by an em-dash and a
277	  specific justification — not the bare token alone; the Verification cell cites a specific
278	  source or names what verification confirms the assumption — not "unclear" or "possibly true";
279	  at least one assumption has been challenged (not merely labelled Accept); if any assumption
280	  is used in a derivation chain despite being unverified, the Verification cell reads
281	  "unverified — flagged"; the Assumption Audit performed at the end of Phase 4 (`SKILL.md`,
282	  "End-of-phase Assumption Audit") visited every named derivation chain step in section 4 and
283	  surfaced any assumption not already in the Assumptions Table, recording it there; the
284	  Assumption Audit artifact produced before scoring (per "How to Apply This Rubric") confirms
285	  this scan was exhaustive over named derivation chain steps, not an open-ended survey of the
286	  universe of conceivable assumptions.
287	
288	- **Sound** — the table exists with populated rows, but one or more rows have generic entries:
289	  the Verification cell reads "unclear" or "unsure" without specifics, OR the Treatment
290	  cell records a treatment that does not match the prescribed treatment for the row's Type,
291	  OR one assumption that is used in a chain despite being unverified lacks the
292	  "unverified — flagged" notation.
293	
294	- **Hand-wavy** — the table exists but uses Type values outside the four-type scheme (e.g.,
295	  "general assumption," "business constraint," freeform labels); OR multiple rows have empty
296	  Verdict or Verification cells; OR every assumption is labelled Accept with no challenge
297	  attempted and no evidence cited for any verdict.
298	
299	- **Absent** — no Assumptions Table is present; OR the table exists but every row's Type
300	  cell is empty, freeform (no mapping to the four-type scheme), or missing — making the
301	  table a list of undifferentiated claims rather than a classified set.
302	
303	### Criterion 3: Establish Ground Truths
304	
305	Scores the **Ground Truths list** — a numbered list of verified facts with stable GT-IDs,
306	source citations, and a provenance label, with unverified and delegate-reported entries marked
307	with the `GT-N?` suffix — in the Ground Truths section (output section 3).
308	
309	**Provenance check (apply before banding).** A citation being present is not verification. For
310	each unsuffixed ground truth, ask whether the analysis read the asserted figure in the cited
311	source — `read-at-source` — or merely received it from a sub-agent, search result, or summary
312	without opening the citation (`reported-by-delegate`, which requires the `?`). Score against
313	what the analysis did, not against how well-formed the citation looks.
314	
315	- **Rigorous** — every GT-item carries a stable identifier (GT-1, GT-2, etc.) that matches
316	  the identifiers referenced in the Derivation Chains section; every verified GT has a source
317	  citation that is more specific than "common knowledge" or "known fact"; every GT carries a
318	  provenance label; every unverified or delegate-reported GT is marked with the `?` suffix;
319	  the `?`-marked GTs are **enumerated by ID** and that enumeration matches the suffixed entries
320	  in the Ground Truths list when checked against it; every unsuffixed GT feeding a
321	  HIGH-confidence chain names its read-at-source location; no assumption that was discarded in
322	  Phase 2 (Verdict: Discard) appears in this list. Every unsuffixed GT whose cited source is
323	  reachable feeds at least one HIGH-confidence chain EXCEPT: the Phase 3 failure record names
324	  the source as unreachable, in which case the GT may feed only MEDIUM or LOW chains, evidenced
325	  by that record naming which source and why unreachable.
326	
327	  **Check the enumeration, do not quote it.** Quoting the analysis's own provenance summary as
328	  the satisfying span does not discharge this criterion — that verifies a summary was written,
329	  not that it is correct. Read the Ground Truths list, collect the IDs actually carrying `?`,
330	  and compare against the enumeration. Cite the comparison as the satisfying span (*"enumerated
331	  GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14; list carries `?` on exactly those four"*). Where a stated count and
332	  its enumeration disagree, the enumeration governs and the mismatched count is itself a defect.
333	
334	  **Reachability is decided by the Phase 3 record, not re-decided here.** A source is reachable
335	  when the Phase 3 verification step opened it, and unreachable when the Phase 3 failure record
336	  names it with a specific reason; the analyst reads the record and does not re-argue
337	  reachability per ground truth. This requirement is not satisfied by a ground truth that feeds
338	  no chain at all — a GT no derivation chain consumes is already a Criterion 4 defect, and the
339	  requirement presupposes at least one load-bearing chain consumes the GT. A single unsuffixed
340	  GT whose reachable source feeds only MEDIUM or LOW chains bands this criterion Sound; the same
341	  shortfall across multiple GTs bands it Hand-wavy.
342	
343	- **Sound** — GT-IDs are present and stable, but one or more verified GTs cite "common
344	  knowledge," "known fact," or no source at all; OR provenance labels are missing though the
345	  `?` suffixes themselves are correctly applied; OR one unread GT (unverified or
346	  delegate-reported) is used without the `?` suffix **and it feeds only MEDIUM or LOW
347	  confidence chains**; OR the `?`-marked GTs are summarized by a bare count rather than
348	  enumerated, though the suffixes in the list are themselves correct.
349	
350	  An enumeration that **disagrees with the list** does not band here — it bands **Hand-wavy**.
351	  A count that merely accompanies a correct enumeration and disagrees with it is a defect but
352	  bands Sound, since the enumeration governs and remains checkable.
353	
354	- **Hand-wavy** — GT-IDs are present but they are not stable (the same ID is used for
355	  different facts at different points in the document, or IDs are renumbered between sections);
356	  OR the list includes an assumption that was assigned a Discard verdict in Phase 2; OR
357	  multiple unread GTs are used in chains without the `?` suffix; OR **the `?` enumeration
358	  disagrees with the Ground Truths list** — an enumeration that omits a suffixed GT understates
359	  the analysis's unverified inputs in the direction that flatters it, and unlike a bare count it
360	  was checkable, so a mismatch is a stronger failure than never enumerating at all; OR **any
361	  unsuffixed GT feeds a HIGH-confidence chain without naming a read-at-source location** — a
362	  HIGH-confidence conclusion resting on a figure nobody read is the failure this criterion
363	  exists to catch, and a single instance is enough to land here.
364	
365	  **Fix — acquire before you downgrade.** Branch one, preferred: acquire the evidence — open
366	  the cited source, per the Phase 3 verification step, and let the read move the provenance
367	  label. Branch two: downgrade the confidence — carry the `?` and drop the chain from HIGH,
368	  taken only when the source cannot be opened or opens without containing the asserted figure or wording. The preference, explicitly: acquisition is preferred when the source is reachable, because a gate whose only available Fix weakens the output resolves every failure toward less claim rather than more evidence. The unreachable case is not a free pass — the downgrade branch still requires the Phase 3 failure record, which source and why unreachable, or `citation does not support the claim`, so a reader can tell a downgrade from a skipped attempt.
369	
370	- **Absent** — no GT-IDs are assigned to any fact in the Ground Truths section; OR the Ground
371	  Truths section lists claims without distinguishing verified from unverified (no `?` suffix
372	  appears anywhere, no citations appear anywhere, and the list is undifferentiated); OR the
373	  section is absent or empty.
374	
375	### Criterion 4: Reason Upward
376	
377	Scores **both** the **Derivation Chains** (output section 4) — one chain per conclusion,
378	formatted as `GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]` with at least one
379	intermediate step — **and** the **Abandoned Reasoning** section (output section 5).
380	Both sections are in scope for this criterion. Quoted span: where the band is determined by chain form or chain dependency, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's chain-form table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Derivation Chains prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Abandoned Reasoning section, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban, a missing `[Assumes: X]` declaration, or hop validity and arithmetic — none of which the chain-form table carries a column for — quote the analysis text directly. Folds in:
381	dead-end honesty, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), escape-valve policing for Abandoned
382	Reasoning (D-03), and hop validity and arithmetic. The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
383	
384	- **Rigorous** — every conclusion stated anywhere in the document (in section 4 or section 6)
385	  has exactly one derivation chain in section 4; each chain names the inputs it consumes — ground truths, upstream conclusions, or both — in the prescribed head form (`GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])`),
386	  contains at least one intermediate claim (a claim that cannot be stated from any single named input alone), and reaches a conclusion; each chain is rendered in the prescribed
387	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. Hops rendered as an ordered list do not satisfy the prescribed form; the Abandoned Reasoning
388	  section either documents
389	  at least one dead end using the What-was-tried / Why-abandoned / What-it-ruled-out structure,
390	  OR uses the honest-depth escape valve with a reason that is specific to this analysis's
391	  problem and appears in no other analysis without alteration; no analogy
392	  is used as direct evidence (any reference to how others solved a similar problem is grounded
393	  in a named GT about their situation, not offered as standalone justification);
394	  each chain step that introduces an assumption not already in the Assumptions Table
395	  declares that assumption inline using `[Assumes: X]` appended to the step text —
396	  a reviewer applies this check by scanning each chain step for the `[Assumes:` token;
397	  and every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by
398	  arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity
399	  cited to an unsuffixed ground truth — the test `output-template.md` states for the HIGH
400	  band under "Confidence levels, defined", shared here rather than restated. A hop that
401	  follows once the `[Assumes: X]` premise declared on that hop is granted counts as following
402	  for this criterion — declaring the premise takes the hop out of this limb by design, and
403	  whether that premise is priced is Criterion 5's Inference axis. An undeclared premise is not
404	  treated that way: a hop the endpoint depends on whose only gap is an undeclared premise is a
405	  non-sequitur under Hand-wavy below, and the `[Assumes: X]` limb above covers undeclared
406	  premises on hops the endpoint does not depend on; a hop citing
407	  a regularity to a `GT-N?` ground truth is an Inputs-axis matter Criterion 3/5 scores, not a
408	  failure to follow.
409	
410	- **Sound** — chains exist for all conclusions, but one or more chains lack a genuine
411	  intermediate step (the chain goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion, or the stated
412	  intermediate is a restatement of one of its named inputs rather than a new inference); OR
413	  a conclusion has more than one derivation chain — redundant restatement rather than a
414	  missing chain — where the prescribed form is exactly one chain per conclusion; OR
415	  one dead end in Abandoned Reasoning is described with a vague abandonment reason
416	  ("seemed unlikely," "ran out of time") rather than the specific structural reason
417	  (assumption false, contradicts a GT, circular, intermediate could not be established); OR
418	  one or more chains render their hops as an ordered list (`1.`, `2.`, `3.`) instead of the
419	  prescribed arrow-led hop form, OR break a single hop across physical lines rather than
420	  splitting it into two hops, which splits one chain into disconnected
421	  fragments even where every hop is individually sound; OR a hop fails to follow, or its
422	  arithmetic does not recompute, where the endpoint does not depend on that hop; OR a hop the
423	  endpoint depends on carries an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged — the
424	  only case of a hop the endpoint depends on that this band admits, and it covers arithmetic
425	  only: a hop the endpoint depends on that does not follow by deduction or cited regularity is
426	  Hand-wavy, whatever the grader judges its effect on the endpoint — **this clause is why the criterion
427	  cannot be scored on reasoning quality alone.** A chain that names its inputs, carries a
428	  genuine intermediate and reaches a conclusion satisfies every other Rigorous requirement
429	  while still failing the prescribed form; scoring only the semantics is what lets a
430	  Rigorous verdict coexist with a section of malformed chains.
431	
432	- **Hand-wavy** — some conclusions lack derivation chains; OR chains reference GT-IDs that
433	  do not appear in the Ground Truths section; OR an analogy is used as direct evidence
434	  ("others have solved it this way," "industry standard is X") without grounding in a named
435	  GT about that other situation; OR the Abandoned Reasoning section uses the honest-depth
436	  escape valve with a reason that is generic and would apply equally to any analysis (e.g.,
437	  "no dead ends were encountered," "all reasoning paths worked"); OR a hop the endpoint
438	  depends on does not follow by deduction or cited regularity (a non-sequitur) — including
439	  a hop whose only gap is an undeclared premise — or an arithmetic error changes the endpoint; an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged
440	  is the Sound clause above, not this one — **this clause is why the criterion cannot be scored
441	  on form alone either.** A chain can name
442	  its inputs, carry a genuine intermediate, render every hop in the prescribed form and reach
443	  a conclusion while a hop the endpoint depends on does not follow.
444	
445	- **Absent** — no derivation chains exist in the document; OR the Derivation Chains section
446	  is absent or empty; OR conclusions appear in section 6 with no corresponding chains in
447	  section 4 — the core question's answer cannot be traced to any named ground truth.
448	
449	### Criterion 5: Validate
450	
451	Scores the **signed-off analysis** — the complete output with all conclusions traced and weak
452	links resolved or explicitly flagged with confidence caveats — across all six output sections,
453	focusing on the confidence caveats attached to the Derivation Chains (output section 4).
454	
455	- **Rigorous** — every derivation chain's weakest link is named; every MEDIUM or LOW confidence
456	  caveat, on a chain or on the Conclusion section, explains only its own rating: it names each
457	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, with the verification that would remove that input as a
458	  cause of the downgrade, and each Cn its head cites — or, for the Conclusion section, each
459	  contributing chain — that is rated below HIGH, and it need not re-explain a named Cn, whose
460	  own caveat carries its explanation; and for each downgrade cause belonging to the chain or
461	  Conclusion itself, such as a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation, it states
462	  what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path
463	  exists, that reason being either, for an absent-fails derivation, the absent-fails EXCEPT
464	  clause below, the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, or an explicit
465	  account of why no available evidence settles that cause;
466	  the overall Conclusion section's confidence rating (HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW) matches the weakest
467	  chain that contributes to it, counting only chains not covered by an EXCEPT clause stated in
468	  this same descriptor; no chain that consumes a GT-N? input is rated HIGH confidence; every
469	  chain is rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites, a ceiling that holds
470	  even when a cited chain is rated MEDIUM under an EXCEPT clause below.
471	  Every rating is calibrated: each chain carries the band its inputs, hops and rivals
472	  license under the three-axis definition in `output-template.md` — no chain rated above
473	  what those axes permit, and none rated below it. A Conclusion claim supported by
474	  at least one HIGH-confidence chain may be presented at HIGH; a claim with no such
475	  chain is presented at the band its weakest contributing chain licenses, and presenting
476	  it so is Rigorous rather than a shortfall. Under-rating is a defect of the same kind
477	  as over-rating, and this criterion scores calibration, not altitude. EXCEPT: a chain is explicitly marked speculative — for
478	  example `[Speculative]` — and the analysis states, in the same place, that the claim it
479	  supports is not load-bearing and is offered for exploration only; that mark plus that
480	  statement is the satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM, though its confidence
481	  line still gives each of its own downgrade causes what would remove it or an explicit account
482	  of why no available evidence settles it, because the mark is not a no-path reason; a
483	  speculative chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing and no longer satisfies this
484	  EXCEPT clause, so a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another
485	  chain's head and instead stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (output section 5).
486	  EXCEPT: a chain is
487	  an absent-fails derivation — of the form "if [assumption] were true we could conclude X;
488	  [assumption] is false; therefore X does not follow" — whose named false assumption is the
489	  satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM because it establishes what does not
490	  follow rather than what does.
491	
492	  The adversarial pass Phase 5 prescribes has run and its record is complete: each computed
493	  figure's recompute, the sensitivity ground truth and whether it is `?`-marked, the rival and
494	  where it is ruled out or carried live, a premise stated in the past tense, an unfiltered
495	  cause list written before any grouping, clusters each naming the chain ids or ground-truth
496	  ids the weakness bears on, per cluster a named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk
497	  with a named mitigation, and the falsification condition — each part present or carrying its
498	  step's not-applicable line. Each structural weakness the pass
499	  returned has landed somewhere a reader can find it — as a named weak link on a chain, or as
500	  an explicit confidence caveat on the conclusion it threatens. An analysis whose conclusion is
501	  neither a plan nor a claim satisfies the Premise, Causes, Clusters and Disposition parts by
502	  carrying the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line with its reason named — that
503	  line is the adversarial-technique step's own not-applicable line, not a waiver of the whole
504	  record, so the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts each still carry their
505	  content or their own step's not-applicable line; an analysis that does carry a plan or a claim
506	  cannot satisfy the technique step that way, and the reason given is what makes the two cases
507	  distinguishable.
508	
509	  **A conclusion without a HIGH chain is not a shortfall.** A conclusion resting on no
510	  HIGH-confidence chain, uncovered by either EXCEPT clause above, is Rigorous on this
511	  criterion when every band it rests on is the band that chain's axes license and the
512	  Conclusion's own rating equals its weakest contributing chain's. A MEDIUM or LOW overall
513	  Conclusion rating remains a legitimate, honestly-caveated analysis — `output-template.md`
514	  permits it and this criterion now scores it Rigorous when it is calibrated. What bands
515	  this criterion below Rigorous is a band that does not match its axes in either direction,
516	  never a band that is merely low, and a verdict block reporting Rigorous alongside a
517	  MEDIUM overall rating is the expected shape of an honest analysis rather than a
518	  contradiction. An exception is claimed, not assumed: an analysis relying on one of the
519	  two EXCEPT clauses above names it in the Criterion 5 verdict block and cites the evidence
520	  that clause requires; an unclaimed exception is not applied on the analysis's behalf.
521	
522	- **Sound** — confidence ratings exist on chains, but a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line omits a
523	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, or a Cn its head cites (or, on the Conclusion section, a
524	  contributing chain) that is rated below HIGH, or a downgrade cause belonging to its own chain
525	  or Conclusion — including a MEDIUM or LOW rating that no named GT-N? input or Cn accounts for
526	  and whose line names no cause of its own; OR a confidence line names a GT-N? input without the
527	  verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; OR a confidence line gives a
528	  downgrade cause belonging to its own chain or Conclusion with neither what would remove it as
529	  a cause of the downgrade nor a permitted no-path reason — for an absent-fails derivation, the
530	  absent-fails EXCEPT clause, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that
531	  cause — including a line whose only account of such a cause is the speculative EXCEPT clause
532	  or any clause other than the absent-fails one; OR a chain's head cites a chain marked
533	  speculative that has no verification path; OR a chain is rated HIGH confidence while consuming
534	  a GT-N? input (the rating does not match the unverified-input rule); OR a chain is rated above
535	  the lowest-rated chain its head cites; OR a single chain's band does not match what its
536	  three axes license, in either direction — a chain rated HIGH whose head carries a `?` or
537	  whose hops rest on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise, or a chain meeting all three axes
538	  rated MEDIUM — while every other chain in the analysis is correctly banded; OR an
539	  adversarial pass record, or the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line, is present
540	  but one or more of the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts is absent and
541	  carries no not-applicable line of its own — a step silently omitted from a pass that otherwise
542	  ran.
543	
544	- **Hand-wavy** — confidence ratings appear on the overall Conclusion section but are absent
545	  from individual derivation chains; OR weak links are described in general terms ("some
546	  assumptions remain uncertain") without naming the specific chain step or GT-N? input that
547	  caused the concern; OR an adversarial pass record is present but no cluster carries a
548	  disposition — neither a named plan change nor an explicitly accepted risk with a named
549	  mitigation — so the pass named structural weaknesses and acted on none of them; OR the record
550	  states its clusters without the cause list they were drawn from, which is the generic risk
551	  list the pass exists to replace rather than a pass that produced one; OR two or more
552	  chains carry bands their axes do not license, so the miscalibration is a pattern rather
553	  than an isolated entry; OR every chain in the analysis carries the same band and no
554	  confidence line names which axis produced it, which is a default setting rather than a
555	  rating.
556	
557	- **Absent** — no confidence ratings appear anywhere in the derivation chains; OR GT-N? inputs
558	  are used in load-bearing chains without any confidence caveat anywhere in the document; OR
559	  — covering the case the first two clauses miss — confidence ratings exist but no weak-link
560	  identification or chain inspection was performed at all, so there is no evidence that
561	  Phase 5's stress-test operation was executed; OR neither an adversarial pass record nor an
562	  `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line appears anywhere in the response, so there
563	  is no evidence that Phase 5's adversarial pass was executed at all. These two clauses are
564	  separate readings: a weakest-link paragraph written by the same reasoning that built the
565	  chains satisfies the first and not the second, and an analysis scoring above Absent on the
566	  strength of that paragraph alone is what this clause exists to catch.
567	
568	### Criterion 6: Conclusion-to-Ground-Truth Traceability
569	
570	Scores the relationship between the **Conclusion section** (section 6) claims and the
571	**Derivation Chains** (section 4) that produced them — a cross-section structural property
572	of the signed-off analysis as a whole. Quoted span: where the band is determined by whether a section-6 claim traces to a named section-4 chain, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's claim-inventory table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Conclusion prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Key Insight being a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a non-obvious finding — a semantic property the claim-inventory table carries no column for — quote the analysis text directly.
573	
574	- **Rigorous** — every claim in the Conclusion section (recommended approach, key insight,
575	  trade-offs acknowledged) traces to a specific named derivation chain in section 4; the
576	  Conclusion section introduces no new claims that did not appear in section 4; the Key
577	  Insight names a non-obvious finding — a result that reasoning by analogy or convention
578	  does not reach — rather than restating the recommended approach.
579	
580	- **Sound** — most Conclusion claims trace to chains in section 4, but one claim is introduced
581	  for the first time in the Conclusion section (new reasoning not present in any derivation
582	  chain); OR the Key Insight is a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a
583	  non-obvious finding.
584	
585	- **Hand-wavy** — the Conclusion section contains claims that contradict or are inconsistent
586	  with the derivation chains in section 4; OR multiple new claims appear in the Conclusion
587	  section that are not present in any derivation chain.
588	
589	- **Absent** — the Conclusion section contains claims with no corresponding derivation chain
590	  anywhere in section 4; OR the Conclusion section is absent or empty; OR every item in the
591	  Conclusion is new reasoning not established by any derivation chain — the Conclusion section
592	  has been used to introduce the analysis's conclusions rather than to synthesize them.
593	
594	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.
595	
596	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
597	
598	A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
599	
600	---
601	
602	## Usage Note
603	
604	Score every criterion. Produce one verdict block per criterion, using the prescribed format
605	from the Verdict Block Format section above. The analysis must clear the gate (no criterion
606	at Absent) and the hand-wavy cap (at most one criterion at Hand-wavy) before conclusions are
607	presented. If either condition is not met, revise the relevant sections and re-score — bounded
608	to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under "How to
609	Apply This Gate" at the top of this document. If a criterion still fails after that single
610	pass, present it as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of re-scoring
611	again. This closing note restates that bound; it does not create a second, looser one.

content.content:
# NIST 800-63B Key Requirements Summary

## Memorized Secrets (Passwords)

**Length Requirements (Section 5.1.1.1):**
"Memorized secrets SHALL be at least 8 characters in length if chosen by the subscriber." CSP-generated secrets require minimum 6 characters.

**Storage (Section 5.1.1.2):**
Passwords must be "salted and hashed using a suitable one-way key derivation function" with at least 32-bit salts. PBKDF2 iteration counts should reach "at least 10,000 iterations."

**Validation (Section 5.1.1.2):**
Systems should reject passwords matching "values known to be commonly-used, expected, or compromised" from breach databases and dictionary sources.

## Rate Limiting/Throttling (Section 5.2.2)

The guideline requires verifiers to "limit consecutive failed authentication attempts on a single account to no more than 100." Additional protective measures include CAPTCHA requirements, exponential wait times between attempts, IP whitelisting, and behavioral analysis tools.

## Multi-Factor Authentication at AAL2 (Section 4.2)

AAL2 mandates either a multi-factor authenticator or "two distinct authentication factors" including a memorized secret plus a possession-based factor (out-of-band, OTP device, or cryptographic software). The protocol must use "approved cryptographic techniques" with authenticated protected channels.

content.content:
# Article 33 GDPR: Breach Notification Requirements

## Time Limit
Controllers must notify the supervisory authority **within 72 hours** of becoming aware of a personal data breach, "unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons." If notification exceeds this window, reasons for the delay must be provided.

## Required Content
Notifications must include at minimum:

- Description of the breach's nature, including affected data subject categories and approximate numbers
- Data protection officer's name and contact details
- Likely consequences of the breach
- Measures taken or planned to address it and mitigate adverse effects

## Additional Provisions
- **Processors** must alert controllers without undue delay after discovering a breach
- Information may be provided in phases if not immediately available
- Controllers must document all breaches with facts, effects, and remedial actions to demonstrate compliance

content.content:
# OWASP Secure Session Management Requirements

## Session ID Generation & Entropy
OWASP mandates that "Session identifiers must have at least 64 bits of entropy to prevent brute-force session guessing attacks." The guidance emphasizes using cryptographically secure random number generators (CSPRNG) to ensure values are unpredictably distributed, making statistical pattern analysis infeasible for attackers.

## Session Fixation Prevention
The framework requires regenerating session IDs after any privilege level change, particularly during authentication transitions. Applications must adopt strict session management—rejecting any session ID not previously generated by the application itself, rather than accepting user-supplied values.

## Cookie Security Attributes
OWASP recommends implementing multiple protective measures:
- **Secure flag**: "instructs web browsers to only send the cookie through an encrypted HTTPS (SSL/TLS) connection"
- **HttpOnly flag**: prevents JavaScript access via `document.cookie`
- **SameSite attribute**: Set to `Strict` (preferred) or `Lax` to control cross-site transmission
- **Cookie prefixes**: Use `__Host-` prefix to enforce `Secure`, absence of Domain, and `Path=/`

## Session Timeout & Expiration
The guidance recommends implementing three complementary mechanisms:
- **Idle timeout** (2-5 minutes for high-value apps; 15-30 minutes for low-risk)
- **Absolute timeout** (4-8 hours for full-day applications)
- **Renewal timeout** (periodic ID regeneration during active sessions)

## Logout & Invalidation
Upon logout or password changes, applications must invalidate sessions server-side using framework methods like `HttpSession.invalidate()`. Client-side actions should clear cookie values and set expiration to past dates. Additionally, use `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Clear-Site-Data` headers to prevent session ID caching.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about SOC 2 Security common criteria and Trust Services Criteria:

## Mandatory vs. Optional Trust Services Criteria

Security is mandatory in every SOC 2 audit, while the inclusion of Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy depends on the services provided and the nature of the data handled.

## Security as Common Criteria

Security — the common criteria, CC1–CC9 — is mandatory in every report; Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy are scoped in based on what you commit to customers.

## The Five Trust Services Criteria

The five Trust Services Criteria are:

1. **Security (Mandatory)**: Security is the baseline for every SOC 2 audit. It ensures systems are protected against unauthorized access, both physical and logical.

2. **Availability (Optional)**: Availability focuses on whether your systems are reliable and accessible when users need them. It evaluates your uptime commitments, disaster recovery processes, and system monitoring.

3. **Processing Integrity (Optional)**: This principle evaluates whether your systems process data accurately, completely, and in a timely manner.

4. **Confidentiality (Optional)**: Confidentiality focuses on protecting sensitive business data from unauthorized access. Think internal IP, financial info, and sensitive customer data.

5. **Privacy (Optional)**: Privacy is all about personal data, how you collect it, use it, store it, and delete it.

Not all TSCs are mandatory in a SOC 2 audit. The criteria you choose to include depend on the nature of your business, customer expectations, and regulatory requirements.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding the fully loaded cost of a senior software engineer in 2026:

## Fully Loaded Cost Estimates

For a Senior SWE, the base salary is $185,000 with benefits and taxes adding $55,500-$74,000, stock/bonus of $60,000-$150,000, resulting in a fully loaded annual cost of $300,500-$409,000 with an employer multiplier of 1.62-2.21x.

Another analysis shows that the real annual employer cost for a senior engineer climbs to $277,000–$427,000, while a senior software engineer with a $150,000 salary costs $195,000-$248,000 in year one once you add benefits, payroll taxes, recruiting fees, equipment and overhead.

## Overhead Multiplier

The most commonly referenced multiplier is 1.5× to 2× multiplier: your actual annual employer cost equals 1.5–2× the base salary, which accounts for employment taxes, benefits, recruiting, onboarding, tooling, and overhead. However, the rule of thumb that a worker costs 1.25x to 1.4x their salary holds at the aggregate level, but tech compensation structures push that multiplier higher at senior levels once equity enters the picture.

## Summary Finding

Full Scale's analysis of 60+ tech companies reveals the average "fully loaded" cost of a US-based senior developer is $285,000 annually when including salary, benefits, overhead, recruitment, turnover, and opportunity costs.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about exporting users and password hashes from Auth0 for bulk migration:

## User Export Portability

User profiles and hashes are portable; Rules, Actions, Hooks, and tenant settings are not and must be rebuilt in the destination. This means while user data can be exported, Auth0-specific configurations cannot.

## Password Hash Export

Bcrypt password hashes can be exported from Auth0 via a support-gated request and imported verbatim into most bcrypt-based destinations, so users keep their passwords. However, there are important limitations:

- Because password hashes are considered sensitive information, Auth0 doesn't export them as part of the general export process. To get the password hashes and other password-related information, you must create an Auth0 support ticket.
- You must be on a paid Auth0 plan to export password hashes.

## Bulk Migration Strategies

Trickle (lazy) migration verifies each password against Auth0 on first login and needs no hash export; bulk migration loads everyone up front and needs the hashes. For bulk migration specifically, password hashes require a support request; not self-serve for all plans.

## Important Note on User IDs

Auth0 user_id values carry connection prefixes, so app-side foreign keys must be remapped through an old-to-new identifier table.

1	<!-- GENERATED — DO NOT EDIT. Source: shared/examples/software-systems-2.md. Regenerate via: scripts/sync-content.py --write. -->
2	
3	# Worked Example: Software and Systems (Build vs. Buy)
4	
5	A complete first-principles analysis of a software-systems decision whose reasoning shape is a
6	capability-cost-risk trade-off rather than a measurement-first bottleneck diagnosis. The
7	question — "build our own authentication, or adopt a managed identity provider?" — is the
8	second SW worked example and is meaningfully distinct from `software-systems.md` (CI/CD
9	pipeline diagnosis). Authored to the standard 6-section output template.
10	
11	**Scenario.** A 7-person engineering team at an early-stage B2B SaaS company (≈$40K MRR,
12	≈120 paying tenants, no enterprise customers yet) is about to ship a feature whose access
13	requires authenticated, per-tenant accounts. Until now the product has run behind a single
14	shared password and a Stripe customer link. The team must choose between (a) building auth
15	in-house on top of an open-source library (sessions, password reset, MFA, audit log) and
16	(b) adopting a managed identity provider — Auth0, Clerk, WorkOS, or similar — and wiring
17	it into the existing service. The CTO has framed the choice as urgent because the gated
18	feature is the next billed release.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## 1. Problem Essence
23	
24	**Core problem:** For this team, at this stage, with this product surface, which of the two
25	viable paths — build auth in-house or adopt a managed identity provider — minimizes the
26	combined cost of capability, ongoing operation, and security/lock-in risk over the next
27	24 months, conditional on a few load-bearing assumptions about the team and the customer
28	trajectory?
29	
30	The triggering framing — "we need auth, what should we pick?" — does not specify which
31	dimension dominates the choice. Both build and buy are technically viable; both have
32	shipped competitors. The first-principles move is to refuse a universal answer (the
33	internet has dozens, all of them context-free), classify the assumptions that actually
34	decide the question, and surface where each path wins. A specific recommendation is
35	produced only after the assumption table is resolved against the team's measured state.
36	
37	**Success criteria:**
38	
39	- The gated feature ships, with working per-tenant authenticated access, within 8 weeks
40	  of the decision — measurable from the deploy log.
41	- Ongoing auth-related operating cost stays within budget for the chosen path: under
42	  ~$400/month for the buy path at the current tenant count, or under ~0.3 FTE of
43	  ongoing maintenance for the build path (incident response, security patches, library
44	  upgrades).
45	- Zero auth-related security incidents in the first 12 months, where "incident" means a
46	  CVE-class vulnerability exploited in production or a credential-exposure event traced
47	  to the auth implementation.
48	- The chosen path does not foreclose the company's known 24-month roadmap: SSO/SAML
49	  support for the first enterprise customer (already in pipeline conversations), and
50	  SCIM provisioning if any enterprise customer requests it.
51	
52	---
53	
54	## 2. Assumptions Table
55	
56	| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
57	|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|
58	| The team can build, harden, and operate session-based auth + MFA + audit log to a security floor acceptable for B2B SaaS without prior in-production auth experience on this team | untested belief — economic-hinge | If false, the entire build-side economic case collapses regardless of headline implementation cost — the team will either ship an under-secured product or absorb a much larger ongoing cost than estimated. Do not enter the decision with this flagged | Challenge — unverified; no engineer on the team has operated production auth before, and this is the load-bearing build-side hinge | Unverified — flagged; nobody on the current team has shipped and operated production auth at this team's previous companies; the assumption is the load-bearing hinge for the build-side TCO |
59	| A managed identity provider's published pricing remains within budget at the team's projected tenant count over a 24-month horizon | untested belief | Verify by walking each candidate provider's published pricing tier against the company's tenant growth projection; flag the specific tier crossings where monthly cost jumps materially | Challenge — partially verifiable via a tier-crossing calculation against published pricing, not a vendor claim | Partially verifiable — Auth0 / Clerk / WorkOS pricing pages and the company's 24-month tenant projection are both available; the verification is a tier-crossing calculation, not a vendor claim |
60	| Migrating off a managed identity provider 18–36 months from now (if pricing trajectory or vendor terms change) is feasible at acceptable cost | untested belief — economic-hinge | If false, the buy path is a one-way door at the moment the first enterprise customer's identity records are stored in the vendor; expiry probability and migration cost must be characterised before signing | Challenge — unverified; export formats are only partially round-trippable, so this is the second economic hinge | Unverified — flagged; user-record export formats are typically supported by the major providers, but social-login linkage, MFA enrollment state, and tenant-specific provider configuration are not always round-trippable; the realistic migration cost is the second economic hinge |
61	| The team's current security posture (no prior CVEs to inherit, no compliance audit yet, no production secrets manager in place) is the floor the auth implementation has to clear | current constraint | Record the floor explicitly; the floor moves up when the first enterprise customer requires SOC2 or signs a DPA with security clauses; the build path then absorbs the cost of meeting the new floor, the buy path inherits the provider's existing posture | Accept — directly observed; the floor and its expiry condition are both documented | Observed: no current compliance audit, no auth-related CVE inheritance, no secrets manager; the floor is documented and the expiry condition (first enterprise customer's security review) is named |
62	| "Roll your own auth" is irresponsible in 2026; reputable engineering practice is to adopt a managed provider | convention — analogy-as-evidence | The claim circulates as a community default but is not grounded in a named ground truth about this team's situation; treat as discarded unless re-expressed as a chain anchored in named GTs | Discard — an analogy-as-evidence move with no named ground truth anchoring it to this team's situation | The claim is an analogy-as-evidence move per `assumption-taxonomy.md`; it may not anchor a chain; the actual question is whether THIS team's specific risk profile clears the security floor for THIS product surface, which the build-vs-buy chains evaluate from named GTs rather than from the convention |
63	| The build-vs-buy decision is binary — adopt one provider fully or build from scratch | untested belief — false-dichotomy | Challenge the binary framing; enumerate intermediate options (e.g., adopt the provider only for login + MFA while owning session, audit log, and tenant model in-house) and check whether any of them dominates either pole on cost, risk, or reversibility | Challenge — a documented hybrid path dominates both poles, discarding the binary framing (chain C3) | The hybrid path — adopt the provider for the high-blast-radius surfaces (password storage, MFA, social login) while owning the lower-risk, vendor-lock-in-prone surfaces (tenant model, audit log, session policy) in-house — is documented in vendor integration guides and is not captured by either of the two original poles |
64	
65	---
66	
67	## 3. Ground Truths
68	
69	- **GT-1** The team comprises 7 engineers; none has shipped and operated production
70	  authentication (session management + MFA + password reset + audit log) end-to-end in
71	  a prior role — source: direct team-experience inventory taken at the start of this
72	  analysis; verified by 1:1 confirmation with each engineer.
73	
74	- **GT-2** The company currently has ~120 paying tenants at ~$40K MRR; the 24-month
75	  projection (used for capacity planning) assumes growth to 600–1,200 tenants and
76	  $200K–$400K MRR, with no enterprise customer requiring SSO/SAML in the next 6 months
77	  but at least one such customer expected in months 9–18 — source: company finance and
78	  pipeline records (CRM-tracked enterprise leads; board capacity-planning model).
79	
80	- **GT-3** As of the analysis date, Auth0 / Okta CIAM, Clerk, and WorkOS publish
81	  per-monthly-active-user (MAU) pricing tiers that include MFA, password reset, social
82	  login, and SOC2-certified infrastructure within their managed offering. Concrete tier
83	  examples on the candidate providers' published pricing pages place the cost for 1,000
84	  MAUs (a midpoint of the 24-month projection if every tenant has 1–2 active users) in
85	  the rough range of $200–$800/month depending on provider, feature mix, and tier — source:
86	  provider pricing pages, retrieved at the analysis date. This ground truth asserts the
87	  price level observed at that date and nothing beyond it: the retrieved values are
88	  published list prices, so they may not reflect negotiated rates or feature bundles, and
89	  any extrapolation across the 24-month horizon is carried by `GT-7?`, not by this entry.
90	
91	- **GT-4** Building production-grade auth in-house — session-based login, secure password
92	  storage (bcrypt/argon2), email-based password reset with rate limiting, TOTP MFA, audit
93	  log of authentication events, account lockout, and basic anomalous-login detection —
94	  is a 4–8 week initial implementation by an experienced engineer using a maintained
95	  open-source library (e.g., the auth library shipped with the team's web framework, or
96	  a dedicated identity library); it is NOT a one-week task and it carries an ongoing
97	  ~0.1–0.3 FTE maintenance cost (security patches, library upgrades, incident response,
98	  CVE monitoring) for as long as it is in production — source: published engineering
99	  retrospectives from similar-stage SaaS companies that have shipped both paths, cross-
100	  referenced against the team-experience GT-1.
101	
102	- **GT-5** A managed identity provider stores user records in its own data model; user
103	  records, password hashes, MFA enrollment state, and tenant-to-user mappings are
104	  exportable for the major providers, but the formats vary by provider and the
105	  round-trippability of social-login provider linkages, MFA enrollment seeds, and
106	  tenant-specific configuration is partial — source: published provider documentation
107	  (data-export endpoints and formats) cross-referenced with engineering write-ups of
108	  documented provider migrations.
109	
110	- **GT-6** The current team has no production secrets manager, no SOC2 audit, and no
111	  documented incident-response playbook for authentication-related incidents; the first
112	  enterprise customer's security review (expected in months 9–18 per GT-2) will require
113	  remediation of these gaps regardless of which auth path is chosen — source: direct
114	  observation of the team's current infrastructure (secret material is in environment
115	  variables in the deploy platform; no audit log of access; no documented IR runbook).
116	
117	- **GT-7?** The specific cost trajectory of any chosen managed provider over the next 24
118	  months is asserted but unverified — list-price snapshots only; the providers reserve
119	  the right to revise pricing tiers, and the actual MAU count at month 24 is itself a
120	  projection — unverified: list prices are a snapshot, not a contract; the 24-month
121	  cost path depends on both the provider's pricing decisions and the actual MAU
122	  trajectory.
123	
124	---
125	
126	## 4. Derivation Chains
127	
128	### Conclusion C1: The build path's headline cost is lower than the buy path at the current MAU, but only if the build-side economic hinge holds
129	
130	GT-4 (4–8 weeks initial build + 0.1–0.3 FTE ongoing maintenance) + GT-3 (managed provider list prices ≈ $200–$800/month at the projected 1,000-MAU midpoint)
131	→ At the current ~120 tenants and an immediate launch budget, the buy path costs approximately $0–$300/month (the lowest tier of most providers covers a small MAU count) and the build path costs 4–8 weeks of engineering time once plus ~0.1–0.3 FTE ongoing; converted at typical fully-loaded engineering cost ($15K–$25K/month per FTE), the build path's ongoing cost is approximately $1,500–$7,500/month — strictly higher than the buy path at every tier through the 24-month horizon's midpoint; the build path's apparent advantage exists only at the initial-implementation one-time cost line, not in the steady-state operating cost; this inverts the common "buy is more expensive" intuition
132	→ The build path's economic case rests on GT-4's lower-bound 0.1 FTE estimate holding, which is itself conditional on the team being able to build and operate auth to the security floor — the load-bearing assumption flagged as `untested belief — economic-hinge` in Section 2. If the team requires 0.3 FTE rather than 0.1 FTE because they hit unfamiliar territory (MFA flow edge cases, account-takeover protections, audit-log correctness for a future compliance audit), the build path's ongoing cost is ~$4,500–$7,500/month and the buy path dominates on cost alone at every tier the 24-month projection crosses.
133	
134	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — downgraded because the chain consumes GT-4's lower-bound and
135	  the unverified team-capability hinge. Raising to HIGH requires either (a) a 4-week
136	  spike on the build path that demonstrates the team is operating at the lower-bound
137	  FTE estimate, or (b) a measured incident in production that disambiguates which
138	  estimate the team is actually at.
139	
140	---
141	
142	### Conclusion C2: The buy path is reversible only if the migration-cost hinge holds, and the reversal window narrows as enterprise customers are added
143	
144	GT-5 (provider data exports are partial — user records yes, MFA enrollment seeds and social-login linkages partial) + GT-2 (first enterprise customer expected in months 9–18)
145	→ Migrating off a managed provider before the first enterprise customer lands is cheap — the team re-issues credentials to ~120 tenants, walks each through an MFA re-enrollment, and accepts the social-login linkage loss as a one-time cost; migrating AFTER the first enterprise customer's identity records (potentially including SAML federation configuration, SCIM provisioning state, and audited access logs the customer has retention requirements on) are stored in the vendor is materially harder — the migration is no longer "re-issue credentials" but "preserve the customer's federation configuration and audit-log continuity through the migration"
146	→ The buy path is reversible at low cost for ≈9 months, becomes a one-way door once the first enterprise customer is onboarded onto the vendor's SSO surface, and stays a one-way door for the rest of the 24-month horizon. The reversal window is the observable, decision-relevant quantity, not the binary "can we migrate?" question. Any future re-evaluation of the buy path must happen inside the 9-month window — after that, the decision is locked in regardless of how the cost trajectory in GT-7? resolves.
147	
148	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — downgraded because the chain consumes GT-7? (pricing trajectory)
149	  and the conditional in GT-2 (first enterprise customer timing is a projection, not a
150	  signed contract). GT-7? would be removed as a cause by a signed contract with the
151	  chosen managed provider pinning the pricing trajectory through the 24-month horizon;
152	  GT-2's conditional would be removed by a signed enterprise customer with stated
153	  SSO/SAML requirements, at which point the reversal window has already closed and the
154	  decision is effectively committed. Both are required, not either — D-07 bars a HIGH
155	  line while any GT-N? input stands, so resolving GT-2 alone leaves this chain at MEDIUM.
156	
157	---
158	
159	### Conclusion C3: The hybrid path dominates the binary framing on the load-bearing security surfaces while preserving optionality on the lock-in surfaces
160	
161	GT-6 (no secrets manager, no SOC2, no IR runbook — the security floor must be cleared regardless) + GT-1 (no engineer on the team has shipped production auth before) + GT-5 (vendor exports are partial; lock-in concentrates where the vendor owns the most state)
162	→ The highest-blast-radius surfaces in any auth implementation are password storage, MFA enrollment, and account-recovery flow — the surfaces where a defect leaks credentials or enables account takeover; these are also the surfaces where the team's inexperience (GT-1) is most expensive: a CVE-class defect here is a company-existential event, not a fixable bug; the lowest-blast-radius surfaces are the tenant model, the audit log, the session policy, and the in-app authorization layer — defects here are recoverable, and these surfaces are also where vendor lock-in concentrates (the tenant model and audit log are exactly the data the vendor "owns" once committed)
163	→ A hybrid path — adopt the managed provider for the credential, MFA, and account-recovery surfaces (where the buy-side capability gap is largest and the lock-in concentration is lowest) while owning the tenant model, audit log, session policy, and in-app authorization in-house (where the build-side risk is lowest and the lock-in cost of buying is highest) — dominates both poles on the joint capability-cost-risk metric. It clears the security floor by delegating the surfaces the team cannot safely build, retains the surfaces the team can safely build and where lock-in would be most expensive, and preserves the migration option at lower cost than the full-buy path because the lock-in-prone surfaces are not stored in the vendor.
164	
165	**Confidence:** HIGH — the chain rests on GT-1, GT-5, and GT-6, all directly observed
166	  rather than projected. The hybrid path's existence collapses the `false-dichotomy`
167	  assumption in Section 2 and reduces the dependence on the two economic-hinge
168	  assumptions.
169	
170	---
171	
172	## 5. Abandoned Reasoning
173	
174	### Dead End: Pure cost comparison over a 3-year TCO model
175	
176	**What was tried:** Compare the two paths purely on total cost of ownership over a
177	36-month horizon. Build a spreadsheet of the build-path costs (initial 4–8 weeks of
178	engineering effort + 0.1–0.3 FTE ongoing maintenance over 36 months at fully-loaded
179	engineering rates) against the buy-path costs (monthly subscription at each tier
180	crossing as MAU grows from ~120 to ~1,000–2,000 over 36 months). Pick the path whose
181	3-year TCO is lower. The motivation was that engineering teams routinely make this kind
182	of build-vs-buy decision via TCO comparison, and the input data (GT-3 on provider
183	pricing tiers, GT-4 on build effort and maintenance burden) is partially available.
184	
185	The TCO model was constructed: at the lower-bound build estimate (0.1 FTE) the build
186	path's 3-year cost is ≈$54K–$90K; at the upper-bound (0.3 FTE) it is ≈$162K–$270K. The
187	buy path's 3-year cost at projected MAU growth is ≈$15K–$40K cumulative at the lower
188	tier crossings and $40K–$100K if the team crosses into the next tier (typically at
189	1,000+ MAUs or when enterprise SSO is enabled).
190	
191	**Why abandoned:** The TCO model produces a defensible-looking comparison whose answer
192	is sensitive to the FTE-loading assumption (the build-side hinge) and the MAU-trajectory
193	assumption (the buy-side cost driver), but it OMITS two costs that the assumption table
194	surfaces as decision-relevant:
195	
196	1. The migration-out cost from the buy path once the first enterprise customer lands
197	   (months 9–18 per GT-2) is not a 3-year-TCO line item — it is a one-time cost incurred
198	   at a future date conditional on a future decision. A TCO model that puts $0 in that
199	   line because no migration is currently planned is implicitly assuming the buy path
200	   will be retained for the full horizon, which is exactly the assumption the chain on
201	   reversibility shows is the load-bearing one. The TCO answer for "buy is cheaper" is
202	   conditional on never wanting to migrate, but the analysis has not established that
203	   the team would never want to.
204	
205	2. The security-incident tail risk on the build path (a CVE-class auth defect from an
206	   inexperienced team, GT-1 + GT-4) is not a 3-year-TCO line item either — it is a
207	   low-probability, high-magnitude event whose expected cost is hard to estimate but
208	   whose realized cost can be a company-existential event for an early-stage SaaS. A
209	   TCO model that puts $0 in that line is implicitly assuming the build-side capability
210	   hinge holds, which is exactly the assumption flagged as `untested belief —
211	   economic-hinge` in Section 2.
212	
213	The TCO answer is therefore a function of two assumptions the TCO model itself does not
214	expose. Abandoned because answering build-vs-buy via TCO alone collapses the analysis
215	back into the assumptions the first-principles framing was supposed to surface. The
216	contingent recommendation from Section 6 is strictly more useful than the TCO point
217	estimate because it names the conditions under which each path is preferred.
218	
219	**What it ruled out:** This dead end establishes that a pure-TCO comparison may not
220	anchor the recommendation for this decision class. TCO is a useful input — it bounds
221	the cost magnitudes — but the answer is over-determined by two unverified assumptions
222	whose treatment belongs in the assumption table, not in a spreadsheet cell. Future
223	build-vs-buy analyses on this team should produce a contingent recommendation first
224	and use TCO to size the cost band of each branch, not to pick the branch.
225	
226	---
227	
228	### Dead End: "We have a senior engineer who built auth before — therefore build"
229	
230	**What was tried:** Reason from an individual engineer's prior auth-building experience
231	(at a previous company, on a different team, at a different stage) directly to a build
232	recommendation. The chain attempted was: a senior engineer on the team has shipped auth
233	once before → that engineer can architect and lead the build here → the team's
234	collective auth capability is sufficient → the build path is safe → choose build.
235	
236	**Why abandoned:** Two reasons surfaced on probing:
237	
238	1. GT-1 documents that NO engineer currently on the team has shipped and operated
239	   production auth end-to-end — re-checking the team-experience inventory specifically
240	   for this dead end confirmed the inventory result. The "senior engineer with auth
241	   experience" turned out, on closer inspection, to have integrated a managed provider
242	   at a prior role (NOT built auth from scratch), and to have authored a session-handling
243	   helper at an even earlier role on a product surface that never required MFA or a
244	   compliance audit. Neither prior experience is the same load-bearing capability the
245	   build path actually requires.
246	
247	2. Even if the prior experience had been a clean match, "this person built it once before,
248	   so we should build" is a `convention — analogy-as-evidence` move per the assumption
249	   taxonomy — reasoning of the form "someone solved a similar problem this way, so we
250	   should too," without the analogue's situation being characterised in terms of a named
251	   GT that links their situation to ours. The taxonomy prescribes Discarding this
252	   pattern as a standalone justification. The prior context had a different team size, a
253	   different threat model, and different compliance obligations. The maintenance burden in GT-4 — security patches, CVE
254	   monitoring, incident response — falls on the CURRENT team, not on the engineer who
255	   shipped auth at a prior company. The single-engineer experience is not transitive to
256	   the team's collective ongoing capability.
257	
258	Abandoned because the chain anchors on an individual-experience claim that does not
259	clear the GT bar (the experience does not match the load-bearing capability) and the
260	assumption-classification step shows the chain shape itself is a convention-as-evidence
261	move that the taxonomy prescribes Discarding.
262	
263	**What it ruled out:** This dead end establishes that "we have someone who has done it
264	before" is not a sufficient anchor for the build path on this decision. Individual
265	prior experience can be a useful input — it lowers the cost of the build-side spike
266	that would verify the economic hinge — but it cannot SUBSTITUTE for the team-capability
267	GT. Any future analysis that attempts to anchor a build-vs-buy decision on an individual
268	engineer's prior work must first re-verify the experience against the actual capability
269	the new context requires, AND must check whether the maintenance burden remains on the
270	same engineer or transfers to a team for whom the experience is not transitive.
271	
272	---
273	
274	## 6. Conclusion
275	
276	**Recommended approach:** (chains C1, C2 and C3) Adopt the **hybrid path** — use a managed identity provider for
277	password storage, MFA enrollment, and account-recovery flows; own the tenant model, audit
278	log, session policy, and in-app authorization in-house. Specifically:
279	
280	1. (chains C1 and C2) Within 2 weeks, select a managed provider whose published pricing tier covers the
281	   projected 24-month MAU range without crossing a tier that materially exceeds the
282	   $400/month budget criterion, and whose data-export surface covers user records
283	   AND audit-log export (the two surfaces the team must be able to round-trip if the
284	   migration-cost hinge later resolves against the buy decision).
285	
286	2. (chain C3) Within 6 weeks, ship the gated feature with provider-backed login + MFA + account
287	   recovery, and in-house tenant model + audit log + session policy + authorization
288	   layer. The gated-feature ship deadline (8 weeks) is achievable on the hybrid path
289	   because the high-risk surfaces (credential storage, MFA) are delegated and the
290	   in-house surfaces are the ones the team can build safely.
291	
292	3. (chain C2) Within 9 months, BEFORE the first enterprise customer's onboarding closes the
293	   reversal window from the Section 4 chain on reversibility, re-evaluate the
294	   migration-cost hinge: rehearse a buy→build migration of the credential surfaces (in a
295	   staging environment, not production) against the chosen provider's data-export
296	   surface, and decide whether the build path is now feasible enough that the team
297	   wants to migrate before the enterprise customer locks in the buy decision.
298	
299	4. (chain C3) Concurrent with steps 1–3 and independent of the build-vs-buy choice: address the
300	   GT-6 gaps (secrets manager, IR runbook, eventual SOC2 path). These are required
301	   regardless of the auth path and represent shared cost the build-vs-buy decision
302	   does not change.
303	
304	**Key insight:** (chain C3) The "build vs buy" framing is a `false-dichotomy` assumption masquerading
305	as the actual decision. The real decision is a per-surface choice: for each auth surface
306	(password storage, MFA, account recovery, tenant model, audit log, session policy,
307	authorization), which path minimizes the joint capability-cost-risk cost on THAT
308	surface for THIS team. The per-surface answer differs across surfaces — the high-risk
309	surfaces favor buy, the high-lock-in surfaces favor build — and the hybrid path is the
310	only path that does not pay the wrong cost on at least some surfaces. The community
311	convention "roll your own auth is irresponsible" is correct about the credential
312	surfaces (where the team's capability gap is largest) and incorrect about the tenant and
313	session surfaces (where the team can safely build and where lock-in would be most
314	expensive). Conflating the two leads to either over-building (incurring the
315	inexperienced-team security risk on the credential surfaces) or over-buying (incurring
316	the lock-in cost on the tenant and session surfaces that the team would have paid less
317	to own).
318	
319	**Trade-offs acknowledged:**
320	
321	- (chain C3) The hybrid path is more architectural work than either pole. The team must define and
322	  maintain the integration seam between the managed provider and the in-house
323	  components (e.g., the provider-issued user identifier becomes a foreign key in the
324	  in-house tenant model; the provider's MFA enrollment state must be synchronized with
325	  the in-house audit log; session expiry policy must be coordinated between the
326	  provider's session and the in-house session). This is genuine ongoing complexity that
327	  the pure-build and pure-buy paths do not carry.
328	
329	- (chain C2) The recommendation defers a hard re-evaluation step to month 9 (before the first
330	  enterprise customer onboards). This defers the binding decision but does not
331	  eliminate it — the team must actually do the re-evaluation, and if the re-evaluation
332	  is skipped, the buy path becomes a one-way door without the team having decided to
333	  walk through it. The Section 4 reversibility chain depends on this re-evaluation
334	  actually happening.
335	
336	- (chains C1, C2 and C3) The recommendation does not produce a universal "build vs buy" verdict — it produces
337	  a verdict contingent on the assumption-table verdicts that hold for THIS team. If
338	  another team applied the same first-principles analysis to the same scenario with
339	  different GT-1 (a team with deep auth experience), GT-2 (no enterprise customers in
340	  the foreseeable horizon), or GT-4 (a smaller security floor because the product
341	  surface does not store regulated data), the contingent recommendation could land on
342	  a different path. The methodology, not the specific verdict, is the transferable
343	  output.
344	
345	**Confidence:** (chains C2 and C3) MEDIUM — the hybrid-path chain itself is HIGH confidence, but the
346	overall recommendation inherits the MEDIUM rating from the chain on reversibility
347	(which depends on GT-7? — the pricing trajectory — and the projection in GT-2 of the
348	first enterprise customer's timing). Raising to HIGH requires both (a) a signed
349	enterprise customer with stated SSO/SAML requirements, which would resolve GT-2's
350	projection into a fact and either confirm or close the 9-month reversal window, and
351	(b) a signed contract with the chosen managed provider that pins the pricing
352	trajectory through the 24-month horizon, which would resolve GT-7?. Either alone
353	leaves C2 at MEDIUM and caps the Conclusion there with it.
354

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own.
